item.title: Why Floating Point Math Causes Inaccuracy and Precision Solutions
item.description:
“Why Floating Point Math Causes Inaccuracy and Precision Solutions”

Why do calculations involving standard floating-point types, such as 35 + (-34.99), yield an imprecise result like 0.009999999999998 instead of the expected 0.01? This common pitfall stems directly from how computers store fractional numbers.

The Core Issue: Binary Representation Limits

Floating-point arithmetic deviates from true real number arithmetic because of finite precision in binary storage.

Imprecision Illustrated

The fundamental problem is that certain decimal fractions (like 34.99 or 0.01) cannot be represented exactly as binary fractions, analogous to how $1/3$ becomes a repeating decimal ($0.333…$) in base 10.

item.title: Solved: Why Does 0.1 + 0.2 Not Equal 0.3 in Programming?
item.description:
“Solved: Why Does 0.1 + 0.2 Not Equal 0.3 in Programming?”

Let’s dive deep into the intricacies of floating-point numbers, uncover the root causes of these discrepancies, and explore robust methods to handle them effectively in your code.

What is the Core Issue with Binary Floating-Point Arithmetic?

The fundamental reason behind 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 lies in the nature of binary floating-point math, which is predominantly based on the IEEE 754 standard . In this system, numbers are represented as a whole number (mantissa) multiplied by a power of two (exponent). This binary representation causes a crucial problem: rational numbers, such as 0.1 (which is 1/10 in decimal), whose denominator is not a power of two, cannot be exactly represented.
